newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Taiwan bond market faces rocky second half.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Taiwan bond market faces rocky second half.

text.p: After several bond yields hit lifetime lows in the second quarter of 1997, analysts say the Taiwan government bond market faces a difficult second half as the blistering stock market shows no signs of slowing.

In 1997, the debt market has boomed only briefly, in late May when the stock market was digesting its big early-year gains and short-term money rates were low -- a combination that sent bond prices soaring.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year 86/4 and 15-year construction bond plunged to record lows.
Since then, the stock market has roared to life again, fuelled by ample liquidity and hopes of a gathering recovery.

The index has risen more than 1,200 points or 15 percent since June 1, 37 percent in calendar 1997 and fully 100 percent since Taiwan's most recent political crisis in March 1996 -- rival China's menacing missile tests in the Taiwan strait.

Dealers say red hot stocks not only are siphoning away funds, crowding out bonds from the money market, but also forcing the central bank to tighten liquidity in a bid to cool what many analysts call a mainly liquidity-driven stock rally.

In June, as the central bank soaked up T$49 billion through negotiable certificates of deposit and T-bills, short-term money rates edged higher and finally skyrocketed into double-digits in the final week of June -- further chilling the debt market.

As daily stock market turnover has blazed numerous times past T$200 billion, peaking at a record T$251 billion on June 19, analysts say there is no sign of when the stock market bulls will finally run out of steam.
BANK TRIES TO COOL SURGING SHARES

Though the central bank has vowed to let the market dictate foreign exchange and money rates, saying intervention was needed only in the face of "abnormal factors", the bank has tried to cool off the soaring turnover and surging share prices by tinkering with liquidity through NCD and T-bill issues.

But by soaking up funds, the bank has only exacerbated an already tight liquidity squeeze -- nudging the overnight interbank rate on June 28 to a seven-year high 11.325 percent. The rate stayed in double digits for nearly a week.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong has all but abandoned the bank's 5.0-5.5 percent target for short-term rates.
Sheu and other bank officials have said there would be no specific target zone for short-term rates and that the bank would continue issuing NCDs to fine tune the money market.
Analysts and dealers say the central bank's attitude will continue to be a key bond market indicator.
If short-term rates are allowed to hover at higher levels for more than just short periods, they say, investors will dump bond holdings to avoid steep repurchase agreement losses.
SHORT TERM RATES TO GO HIGHER IN SECOND HALF
More than 90 percent of bond market turnover is conducted through repo and little via outright buying and selling.
If the spread between repo rates and bond yields reverses to become negative arbitrage, traders can be expected to sell off their bond holdings aggressively, analysts said.
Several economists told Reuters that they expect short-term rates to go higher in the second half, though there was no consensus about where the new range would be.
Most experts agree it depends on how high stocks fly.
A senior dealer at a major state-run bank, who asked not to be identified, predicted short-term rates might range between 6.50 and 7.50 percent as long as share prices are surging.
President Securities chief economist Martina Yu said a number of market and political factors would squeeze liquidity through the end of 1997.

"Traditionally, liquidity is a bit tight in the third quarter and the county governor elections in the fourth quarter will create strong cash demand," Yu said. "The whole picture for second half liquidity still looks gloomy."
INFLATION TO STAY BELOW THREE PERCENT
Though the interest rate uptrend seems bearish to the bond market, some dealers point to some positive factors that could prevent bond yields from rising too sharply.
These bullish factors include a short supply of bonds, a persistently low inflation rate and a promised reduction of banks' reserve requirements, dealers said.
According to the central bank, the inflation should stay below three percent for all of 1997, something that will be welcomed by the fixed income market.
"The chips (bond supply) problem is the bulls' ace as the amount of bonds maturing outnumbers bonds issuing before year-end," said Grand Cathay Securities dealer Daniel Lee.
"Long-term investors still need the chips in their portfolios after their holdings mature, so they could be the potential buyers in the secondary market."

The Finance Ministry has said it will issue T$70 billion in bonds in the fiscal year to June 1998, while bonds worth T$109 billion will mature in the same period, which would replenish liquidity if the ministry sticks to the plan.
The central bank has said repeatedly it will lower reserve requirements in keeping with international norms, promising to do so before year-end.
Dealers say they expect the central bank to raise banks' liquid reserve ratio at the same time that it cuts reserve requirements, which also would help the debt market.

"Banks are expected to retain large amounts of funds to park in bonds as the liquid reserve ratio is raised," said Lee. "If the stock market takes a break later this year, strong demand as well as short supply will provide room for yields to fall."
